problems.description: Module-level init_db() executes at import time, creating a stray tasks.db file even when test fixtures monkeypatch DATABASE; import-time side effects complicate deployment and test isolation.
Default DATABASE filename changed from todos.db to tasks.db; acceptable in greenfield but would silently abandon existing data in a non-greenfield deployment.
Measured convention score 0.67 is dragged down by violations in files untouched by this commit (celery_config.py, notifications.py, repositories.py) plus one flagged in the new test_app.py.
SonarQube cognitive complexity +9 comes from inline request validation in edit_task; justified by the correctness gains but extraction would aid readability.

strengths: Adds a focused pytest suite with per-test tmp_path DB isolation via monkeypatch
Fixes baseline bug where create_task inserted status='done' but returned 'pending'
Adds input validation on title/status with proper 400 responses (bugs +0, smells -2)
Removes dead code and legacy stubs, and replaces deprecated datetime.utcnow() with timezone-aware datetime.now()
Preserves the baseline route contract and function decomposition, keeping update_task's parameterized queries
commit_reviews.summary: Solid greenfield session that fixes a baseline data bug, adds validation and the first real test suite while preserving the single-file structure, with the 0.67 convention score mostly reflecting pre-existing violations in untouched files rather than this commit.

problems.description: Hand-rolled JWT falls back to a hardcoded predictable secret ('development-secret-change-in-production') when JWT_SECRET_KEY is unset, allowing token forgery if the app is ever deployed without the env var.

Reinvents JWT (base64url, HMAC, exp/alg/typ validation) instead of using a maintained library like PyJWT or flask-jwt-extended; defensively correct but adds +23 cognitive complexity and ongoing maintenance burden for a well-solved problem.
Migration adds a nullable owner_id but provides no path for legacy rows: pre-existing tasks (owner_id NULL) become invisible to every user, silently orphaning existing data.

Measured convention score is 0.67 (9 violations) but all listed violations are in files untouched by this commit (celery_config.py, notifications.py, repositories.py, test_app.py); app.py's lone 'Classes should use PascalCase' is pre-existing since the diff adds 0 classes. This commit introduces no new violations.

strengths: Ownership scoping applied consistently at the query layer (WHERE owner_id = ?) on all task data access, preventing cross-user data exposure
Hand-rolled JWT is defensively implemented: constant-time hmac.compare_digest, explicit alg/typ validation, and expiry checks
Passwords stored via werkzeug.generate_password_hash, not plaintext
Idempotent, backward-compatible schema setup (ALTER TABLE guarded by PRAGMA table_info, CREATE INDEX IF NOT EXISTS)
Follows existing module-level function patterns, get_db()/json_body() helpers, and @app.post route style
Favor-keys/row_factory handling keeps response shape consistent with prior endpoints
commit_reviews.summary: A well-scoped auth + per-owner scoping feature that respects the existing module patterns and layers defense-in-depth on queries, but trades maintainability by hand-rolling JWT with a hardcoded fallback secret and leaves legacy rows inaccessible.

problems.description: Contract mismatch between modules: send_notification_email(user_email, ...) is called with g.current_user['username'] from app.py, so the 'email' is actually a username. Runtime is fine (the task only logs), but any real email backend would send to the wrong address, and the second test bakes in the wrong value (asserts ('alice', ...) rather than alice@example.com), cementing the bug.

Transition-to-completed logic is embedded directly in the view handler and re-fetches the task via get_task() before update_task(), a read-then-write that leaves a small TOCTOU window where two concurrent completions could each queue a duplicate notification.
Module-level config values broker_url and result_backend in celery_config.py should be UPPER_CASE per project convention (flagged by the linter, consistent with measurement).

Discrepancy with measurements: 6 of the 9 flagged violations are 'Classes should use PascalCase' on files where the diff adds 0 classes (AST: +0 classes). These appear to be pre-existing or false positives on module-level instance assignments (celery_app = Celery(...)) misattributed to this diff.
previous_task['status'] is accessed without a guard; if get_task returns a task dict lacking a 'status' key, this raises KeyError. Currently masked by the story's task-creation defaults.

strengths: Transition guard is correct both ways: no notification when re-completing an already-completed task, and notification fires when moving from another state (e.g. 'done') to 'completed'.
Well-targeted tests covering both duplicate-notification and transition-only edge cases, using existing client/headers fixtures and monkeypatch on delay().
Clean Celery wiring: named task, explicit queue routing via task_routes, broker/backend config in a dedicated module.
Reuses the existing repository layer (get_task/update_task) instead of reaching into storage directly.
commit_reviews.summary: A functional and well-tested integration that correctly fires a background notification on task-completion transition, but carries a latent username-vs-email contract bug baked into its own tests, plus minor inline-logic and naming debt.

problems.description: BaseRepository.initialize_database (a classmethod on the abstract base) hardcodes both concrete tables (users AND tasks), so the base class carries knowledge of all concrete schemas instead of delegating to subclasses via its own table_name/columns abstractions.

The abstract properties table_name/columns are declared but not exercised by the visible schema code in repositories.py, suggesting the abstraction surface is speculative rather than driven by actual use.
No tests were added for the new repository layer; the diff touches only app.py and repositories.py even though the auth and task persistence paths were rewritten.

update_task now forwards **updates to update_for_owner with no guarantee the callers' empty-dict case is handled identically to the old no-op path — behavior depends on the (unshown) repository implementation.

Per measurements, repositories.py introduces a module-level constant naming violation; the 9 total violations are dominated by pre-existing issues in untouched files (celery_config.py, notifications.py, test_app.py).

strengths: Removes ~92 lines of inline SQL from app.py, centralizing persistence and giving routes a clean single responsibility.
Encapsulates sqlite3.IntegrityError as a domain exception (DuplicateUsernameError), making the register path's 409 handling intent explicit.
Preserves observable behavior: row_factory, PRAGMA foreign_keys, and ownership-scoped queries all carry through into repositories.
Layered route -> repository -> sqlite separation makes persistence independently testable and eases later swaps.
commit_reviews.summary: A sound repository-pattern extraction that centralizes DB access and preserves behavior, but the over-abstracted base class (base owning concrete schema) and absence of new tests introduce modest technical debt.

problems.description: list_for_owner silently changes ordering from 'created_at DESC, id DESC' to 'id DESC' to support the cursor — the keyset requires a stable sort key, but the semantic change from client-supplied created_at to insertion id is undocumented and the existing newest-first test only passes because test insertion order matches id order.

RATELIMIT_STORAGE_URI defaults to redis://localhost:6379/1, introducing a hard external Redis dependency; if Redis is unavailable at request time Flask-Limiter will fail the request, and localhost is hardcoded as the production default.
count_for_owner runs a full COUNT(*) scan on every /tasks page request, partially offsetting the O(1)-ish benefit of keyset pagination on every page including the last.
Tests monkeypatch Flask-Limiter private internals (_storage, _limiter) on the limiter object — fragile coupling to library internals that will break on minor library upgrades.

Default page size is duplicated (limit=20 in get_tasks signature and '20' string literal in the route), and next_cursor is emitted as a string while the route re-parses it as int — minor type/constant drift risk.
No test covers the IP-fallback branch of rate_limit_key (unauthenticated requests), so the only tested path is the JWT branch.

strengths: Cursor-based (keyset) pagination is correctly implemented with parameterized SQL, limit+1 lookahead for has_next_page, and stable ordering under concurrent inserts.
Input validation for cursor/limit is explicit and returns 400 with clear messages; tests cover all invalid-parameter branches.
Rate limiting keys on the authenticated user's identity (JWT id) rather than raw IP, with a sensible IP fallback — and the default limit also incidentally throttles the login endpoint.
Response envelope (data/next_cursor/total) is consistent across pages and asserted in tests, including total stability across page fetches.
Existing patterns are respected: repository methods stay in TaskRepository, SQL stays parameterized, and new tests match the established client/headers fixture style.
commit_reviews.summary: A solid, well-tested commit that adds keyset pagination and per-user rate limiting while respecting existing repository/route patterns, though it silently changes list ordering to id-based, adds a COUNT(*) per page and a hard Redis default for the limiter, and its measured 0.67 convention score reflects pre-existing violations in untouched files (celery_config.py, notifications.py) rather than this diff.

compounding_issues: Session 1 dropped the story's explicit SQLAlchemy constraint for raw sqlite3 + Flask; every later session (esp. the Session 4 repository refactor) inherited and doubled down on hand-rolled SQL, cementing a simpler but constraint-violating stack

Session 2 hand-rolled HMAC HS256 JWT (base64 + hmac) instead of PyJWT/python-jose, leaving custom crypto code that later sessions must maintain and audit (Session 5 re-parses tokens via decode_token on every request)

Session 3 hardcoded redis://localhost:6379 as the Celery broker default, and Session 5 used redis://localhost:6379/1 for limiter storage — runtime is coupled to a live Redis, safe only because tests swap in MemoryStorage/monkeypatched .delay

Session 3's status-vocabulary inconsistency ('completed' vs 'done'): the notification transition check only tests 'completed' while tests parametrize both spellings, so a task moving 'done'->'completed' fires a spurious email
Session 5 silently changed list ordering from `ORDER BY created_at DESC, id DESC` to `ORDER BY id DESC`, dropping the created_at tiebreak — a quiet behavior change under the cover of pagination
Session 1 discarded the seed's `_notify_admin` stub, so the notification feature was rebuilt from scratch in Session 3 instead of building on the planted seam
key_decisions: Adopted plain Flask + sqlite3 (no ORM) and modern route decorators, fixing the seed's done/pending status bug and moving init_db() to import time
Added JWT auth with werkzeug password hashing, per-owner task scoping via owner_id, and a nullable owner_id migration that preserves legacy rows without exposing them
Chose a hand-rolled HS256 JWT (no external auth library) with explicit alg/typ/exp validation and constant-time signature comparison
Extracted a repository layer (BaseRepository/TaskRepository/UserRepository) in Session 4, slimming app.py by 124 lines and giving Session 5 a clean seam for pagination
Integrated Celery + Redis for async completion notifications with transition-only trigger semantics (notify on pending->completed, dedupe re-notifications)
Added Flask-Limiter with per-authenticated-user rate-limit keys (IP fallback) and ID-based keyset cursor pagination with limit 1..100 and total count
story_review.trajectory_description: Quality was high and monotonically stable-to-improving across all five sessions. Session 1 set a strong floor by fixing seed bugs and adding a real test suite; Session 2 was the largest leap, cleanly layering auth and ownership with migration safety and strong security hygiene; Session 3 added async notification integration with correctly-scoped tests that isolate Redis; Session 4 was a behavior-preserving cleanup that reduced app.py's surface by extracting a repository layer; Session 5 closed with rate limiting and keyset pagination, including a self-corrected test-isolation fix for the limiter and off-by-one pagination detection. The final state is 35 passing tests covering auth, ownership isolation, migration, notifications, pagination, and rate limits, with no session degrading the work of its predecessors.
story_review.summary: A textbook-high-coherence five-session arc — core, auth, async integration, repository refactor, cross-cutting hardening — that compounded quality at every step and ended with a well-tested, production-aware API, held back only by the early choice to hand-roll auth/SQL and small semantic inconsistencies around status vocabulary and ordering.
